name: Tunzu
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Blench, Roger & John Garah Nengel. 2004. Notes on the Tunzu (Duguza) people and language. Ogmios (Newsletter of the Foundation for Endangered Languages) 2.11 (#23), Spring 2004 (dated 30 April 2004): 16-17. (Same text as the 2-pp. 'Notes on the ' on rogerblench.info = Glottolog's only descriptive item, listed by Glottolog as a minimal description.)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Sociolinguistic/ethnographic note only (classification, name etymology, population, villages, migrants, endangerment). The words stress, accent and tone do not occur; the only prosodic information is tone marks on the name forms (Tunzú 'one person', àTunzû 'people', ìTunzû 'language'). p.16: 'There appears to be no published data on the language at all.'

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2021. Introduction to the Shammɔ peoples of Central Nigeria. Draft ms., Jos, 12 May 2021, 12 pp. (Glottolog ref 586185; academia.edu 48907913).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 2.7 Tunzu [=Duguza], p.10, repeats the 2004 note: 'There is no published data on Tunzu and no language development. An informal wordlist taken in 2003 suggested Tunzu is close to Boze.' No phonology, tone or stress for Tunzu.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2020. The East Kainji languages of Central Nigeria. Afrika und Übersee 93: 45-92. DOI 10.15460/auue.2020.93.1.210 (open access).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Tunzu, which appears only in the survey list (p.47), Table 1 (p.49: 'Tunzu | Vigorous | Blench (2004)') and the classification tree. Sec. 3.1 Phonology (pp.54-58) describes ɛBoze only: 'All East Kainji languages so far studied have a relatively simple phonology and broadly resemble one another'; 'Boze has four level tones as well as rising and falling tones'; 'Other East Kainji languages have much reduced systems'. The word 'stress' occurs nowhere in the article.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2020. An Atlas of Nigerian Languages, edition IV (version 11 Sept 2020). Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. Entry 448 'Tunzu'.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Entry gives names (Tunzú / àTunzû / ìTunzû; Dugusa, Duguza), location, 2500 speakers (Blench 2003 est.), classification 'Eastern Kainji: Northern Jos group: group c', 'Threatened by switch to Hausa', 'Source(s) Blench & Nengel (2003)'. No wordlist, phonology or grammar reference is listed for Tunzu.

sources.note: Nothing on Tunzu: it occurs only in classification lists ('Tunzu (=Duguza)'), an empty row of the 'arm/hand' comparative table, and a photo caption ('Tunzu horn players'). Their phonology sections cover Boze/Gbiri only; no stress statement for any East Kainji language.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2003. Tunzu (Duguza) wordlist, taken 30 December 2003 (unpublished field data; cited as 'an informal wordlist taken in 2003' in Blench & Nengel 2004 and Blench 2021).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: The only linguistic data on Tunzu that exists; if tone-marked it would be the sole primary evidence on Tunzu prosody. Never posted on rogerblench.info (the Internet Archive's index of the East Kainji folder lists only 'Notes on the '); Blench 2020 Table 1 sources Tunzu to 'Blench (2004)', not to the 2016 survey data release.

sources.citation: Crozier, David & Roger M. Blench. 1992. An Index of Nigerian Languages, 2nd ed. Dallas: SIL. (entry Duguza)

sources.note: Classification source cited by Blench & Nengel 2004; Index entries list existing wordlists/grammars and would confirm that none existed for Duguza in 1992. Not expected to say anything about stress.

sources.citation: Shimizu, Kiyoshi. 1982. Die Nord-Jos-Gruppe der Plateausprachen Nigerias. Afrika und Übersee 65(2): 161-210 (with 1979 'Five wordlists' AuÜ 62: 253-271 and 1982 'Ten more wordlists' AuÜ 65: 97-134).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: The only comparative phonology of the Northern Jos (East Kainji) group, with reconstructed tones (H, L, downstep for Proto-North-Jos per Blench 2020); Blench & Nengel state Shimizu published no Tunzu data, so at most it gives the group-level tonal frame, not a Tunzu statement.
